titulo.texto: The Red Temples and the House of the Eagles

frase_gancho.texto: Two small temples with traces of paint, an L-shaped building, and a hailstorm that changed everything in two thousand twenty-one.

puente_narrativo.texto: At the end of the walkway, enter the museum and stop in the lobby, where the great sculpture of the earth goddess stands.

guion_corto.texto: Before you reach the museum, the walkway shows you two groups of smaller buildings that stood alongside the pyramid. First, the Red Temples: one to the north, Building C, and another to the south, Building F, each under a roof covering of about ninety square meters. According to the INAH, the one in the north courtyard is a small building, inspired by constructions from Teotihuacan, with mural painting on stucco, and it dates to around fifteen hundred, during the reign of Ahuítzotl. Next, the House of the Eagles, an L-shaped building that the INAH dates to around fourteen eighty. In nineteen ninety-four, two figures of Mictlantecuhtli, the god of death, were found here. On April twenty-eighth, two thousand twenty-one, a hailstorm severely damaged the roof covering that protected it, and the site reopened on November fifteenth, two thousand twenty-two, with a new roof.

guion_largo.texto:
Until now you have been looking at the main pyramid, but the Templo Mayor was only the largest building in a much greater complex. At this stop you are going to see two groups of smaller structures that surrounded it: the Red Temples and the House of the Eagles.

The sacred precinct of Tenochtitlan had temples, platforms, schools, and priests' houses. The Templo Mayor stood at the center, and around it were buildings dedicated to other gods and to different functions. Of that complex, archaeology has recovered only a part. The rest lies beneath colonial and modern streets and buildings, and it cannot be excavated without damaging them.

Let's begin with the Red Temples. They are two small buildings preserved under a roof. They are identified by letters: the North Red Temple is Building C, and the South Red Temple is Building F. Each has a roof covering of about ninety square meters, which protects them from the sun and the rain. Notice that they are much smaller than the pyramid: they were not the great sanctuaries, but part of the spaces that surrounded it.

According to the INAH, the Red Temple in the north courtyard is inspired by constructions from Teotihuacan, the great ancient city that the Mexica admired. It preserves mural painting on stucco, with designs and colors that give meaning to its name. The small buildings of that courtyard date to around fifteen hundred, in Stage six of the Templo Mayor, during the reign of Ahuítzotl, between fourteen eighty-six and fifteen hundred two. What each one was used for is still under study, so it is wise to treat any overly confident explanation with caution.

Remains of another building of the precinct were also found. Where the Centro Cultural de España stands today, at one side of the site, what is interpreted as a calmécac came to light, a school for young people from noble families, where they were trained to become priests or leaders. For the Mexica, knowledge also had its own place within the precinct, next to the temples.

Now look at the House of the Eagles, one of the most important buildings of the precinct after the pyramid. Its story includes a discovery, a loss, and a recovery.

According to the INAH, it was built around fourteen eighty. Other studies give a broader range, between fourteen thirty and fifteen hundred two, so the safest approach is to place it in the second half of the fifteenth century. The name is related to eagles: in this building, a ceramic figure of an eagle warrior was found.

The building is L-shaped and measures about fifty-two meters by thirty-two. It is not entirely in view: half of it lies beneath Justo Sierra Street and beneath the Porrúa bookstore. In other words, part of the Mexica building still lies under the modern city.

In nineteen ninety-four, two large figures of Mictlantecuhtli, the god of death, were found in tunnels beneath the street. They measure one meter seventy-four and weigh about one hundred twenty-eight kilos. The museum displays one figure of Mictlantecuhtli in the Huitzilopochtli Hall. That same hall holds the figure of the eagle warrior, which the archaeologist Leonardo López Luján prefers to call eagle man.

On April twenty-eighth, two thousand twenty-one, a heavy hailstorm severely damaged the roof covering that protected the building. According to an INAH bulletin, a new roof covering of about eight hundred square meters was installed, and the site reopened to the public on November fifteenth, two thousand twenty-two. A roof covering protects the remains from rain and sun, but it can also fail, as happened here. The archaeological zone sits in the middle of a city, and it has to be cared for every day.

What exactly the House of the Eagles was used for is still under study. What is clear is that an eagle warrior and two figures of the god of death were found here together, two themes that the Mexica associated with war and with the final destiny of people. Lean out from the walkway, look for the remains of walls and steps, and compare what you see with the figures you will see later in the museum.

When you are finished, continue to the next stop on your tour.

texto.Red Temples of the north courtyard: around 1500, Stage VI, reign of Ahuítzotl, according to the INAH
texto.House of the Eagles, date: around 1480 according to the INAH; other studies give 1430 to 1502

texto.pregunta: Myth: The House of the Eagles is complete and fully in view.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Part of it lies beneath Justo Sierra Street and a bookstore, and its roof covering suffered severe damage in 2021.
